issue: The repaired statement holds as written. I found no false claim in (a), (b) or (c). (a) In a slice category the identity is terminal, and pt is initial in Diff_*, so both claims and the uniqueness of rho_M are immediate. (b) A product in a slice is a pullback over the base. The forgetful functor from the coslice pt/Diff to Diff creates all limits, and the induced map is pointed because limit projections are jointly monic. Testing in Meth against pointed two-point 0-manifolds shows that whenever a product exists, its canonical map to Q_M x Q_N is a bijection onto the set-level fibre product, so Im(MxN) = Im M ∩ Im N. An embedded-submanifold fibre product, which covers both the clean and the affine case, is a pullback in Diff. The transversality dimension count is right. (c) Functoriality, the choice-based set-level lift, and the cube-root counterexample are all correct. The t^3 vs u^5 remark in "What this explains" is also correct: the lift t^(3/5) is not C^1, and the reverse lift u^(5/3) is C^1 but not C^2, so the two methods are incomparable. The defects that remain are presentational, plus one small proof gap. (1) The statement justifies the non-existence of LoRA_1 x Frozen by saying the cross {BA=0} "is not a manifold". That is a non sequitur. A putative product P need not carry the subspace topology, and the cross is the bijective image of a manifold under an injective immersion: R ⊔ (R\{0}) maps onto the two axes, minus the duplicated origin. What actually rules out P is the universal property, which the proof uses correctly. (2) The proof lifts both axis curves "through the base point of P". That only works if LoRA_1 is pointed at (0,0). The statement leaves the pointing unspecified. For the paper's default T_A-type pointing (B_0,A_0) = (0,a_0) with a_0 ≠ 0, the axis {A=0} does not pass through the base point. The argument must use p* = the unique point of P over the origin, together with unpointed test objects, made pointed as R ⊔ pt or by a smooth flat-cornered curve through both points. Also, "dim P" should mean the local dimension at p*. A cleaner argument: the smooth lifts of both axes through p* force rank(d iota)_{p*} ≥ 2. A small ball around p* then has constant rank 2, so by the constant rank theorem its image contains an open subset of R^2, which the cross does not. (3) "PEFT regime" is undefined. The transversality sentence should say "whenever |M|+|N| < dim Theta". Numerical checks (numpy) agree: the I.8(a) fibre product has dimension 4 = r^2 at (6,8,2); |M|+|N| = 28 < 48 = dim Theta, so transversality fails there; the difference quotients of the cube-root and t^(3/5) lifts blow up at 0; and an injective immersion onto the cross exists.

Take Theta = R and LoRA_1: (B,A) -> theta_0 + BA, pointed at (0,a_0) with a_0 ≠ 0, the T_A-type pointing. The curve t -> (t,0), which traces the axis {A=0}, never passes through the base point (0,a_0). The map from R ⊔ (R\{0}) to R^2, sending s to (0,s) on the first piece and s to (s,0) on the second, is an injective immersion of a manifold onto the cross. So "underlying set = cross, which is not a manifold" does not by itself rule out a product.

safe_public_statement: In the pointed slice category of weight-space PEFT methods over (Theta, theta_0), the frozen model is initial and full fine-tuning is terminal. Two methods have a categorical product whenever their fibre product exists in Diff, for example when it is an embedded submanifold, as it is for affine parametrisations like the one-sided LoRA pair that yields LoRA-XS. The stated formula does not.

(2) The sentence 'Strong monoidality is relative to the permutation groupoid, not to discrete N' is true only for SYMMETRIC strong monoidality. (3) The claim that r↦LoRA_r with standard pointings is not strong monoidal concerns a functor that cannot exist on all of N, because T_A requires r<min(m,n) (Thm II.2). So the obstruction is exactly the reuse of the same object, and that is the only case the proof uses. The proof is correct but does not say this.

The core corollary is true and its proof is complete. If W = W_0 R with R in O(n), then K_out(W) = K_out(W_0) and the singular values are unchanged. Products of orthogonal matrices stay orthogonal, so this survives merge-and-restart cycles. A block-diagonal R with a fixed partition fixes every W_{:,J}W_{:,J}^T. The Cayley–Neumann identity R = (I+Q)(I+Q+Q^2+Q^3) = C(Q)(I-Q^4) is right, and so are R^T R = RR^T = (I-Q^4)^2. Four problems remain.

(1) The coverage list misleads about GOFT as released. In the official code (github.com/ArthurLeoM/peft-givens, tuners/givens), the defaults are strict_oft=True and no_scaling=False. With these defaults update_layer creates a trainable givens_scaler g in R^{in_features}, initialised at ones. The forward pass rotates x, then multiplies by g, then applies W_0. So W = W_0 diag(g) G and K_out(W) = W_0 diag(g)^2 W_0^T, whatever the Givens part G is. Neuron norms, cosines and the spectrum all move. This is the paper's 'GOFT*' ablation, a learnable diagonal on top of the rotation. Only GOFT with no_scaling=True, or as written in the paper, is covered. This is the same kind of default-implementation gap that the first round fixed for HF's Cayley–Neumann OFT. Side note: ETHER's code has a flip_side option (default False) that moves it to the output side, where K_in is preserved instead of K_out.

(2) The BOFT remark says cosines are preserved 'iff s in T_m^+'. That is false; the referee note's 'exactly iff s > 0' is wrong for the same reason. Since cos'_ij = sign(s_i s_j) cos_ij, any s with all entries negative also preserves every cosine. The claim that |cos| is preserved also needs s_i != 0; boft_s is an unconstrained real, so s_i = 0 kills that neuron and its angles are undefined. The clause 'preserves diag(s)W_{:,J}W_{:,J}^T diag(s)' does not parse, because a quantity that depends on s cannot be 'preserved'.

(3) The criterion 'a single non-conformal 2x2 block already changes the cosine' implies that conformal blocks are harmless. That is false when n > 2. A scaled rotation sqrt(c)·Rot with c != 1 on two of the n input coordinates generically changes cosines.

(4) The Cayley–Neumann remark and the headline both need qualifying. The drift is already present in the adapted, unmerged weight, not only 'per merge'. The singular values of R are |1-theta_k^4|, so R is singular whenever some rotation angle theta_k = 1. The C(Q) = (I+Q)(I-Q)^{-1} used here equals C(-Q) in HF's exact-branch convention, (I-Q)(I+Q)^{-1}. The headline 'never change the spectrum, however often they are merged' holds only in exact arithmetic.

The correct condition is X = F(W0 C W0^T)·W0, that is, left multiplication by a matrix-valued function of the output second moment.

(4) The two-sided whitening "with an output second moment" is degenerate. Some independent output-side statistic, such as a gradient second moment, is required.

The sentence also contradicts itself: the image depends on the rank allocation it calls only CO(n)-covariant.

Its cross-paired U_{r:2r} and V_{:r} also make the split depend on the SVD sign convention.

In causal decoders whose content positions are offset by the prompt length in both methods, every soft prompt is reproduced exactly by the deep prefix made of its own per-layer keys and values (cf. Petrov–Torr–Bibi 2024, §2.2). For generic frozen weights (in a bias-free head, W_o != 0 and W_q != 0 suffice), a prefixed vanilla softmax head is not affine on length-one inputs, so prefix tuning cannot be merged box-locally into a standard attention head.

But Petrov–Torr–Bibi 2024, Sec. 2.2, already gives the construction almost word for word, in the same paper the theorem cites for (c): "every soft prompt ... can be represented as a prefix by setting the deeper prefixes to be the values that the model would compute at these positions". Their soft-prompt definition, Eq. 4, already places content at positions n_S+1, ..., so the offset convention is built in. Li & Liang 2021, Sec. 7.2 ('embedding-only' ablation: "the upper activation layers are computed by the Transformer") gives the same inclusion informally. Only the categorical typing (an arrow in the slice over the realisation) and the explicit HF hypotheses are new.

(2) 'WHAT THIS EXPLAINS' MISSTATES THE LITERATURE. It calls "whether the inclusion is strict" an open question. Petrov et al., Sec. 2.2, state "The reverse also does not hold ... prompting < soft prompting < prefix-tuning", and Li–Liang, Sec. 7.2, state "discrete prompting < embedding-only ablation < prefix-tuning". Strictness is also easy in a toy case. Take a one-layer head with one virtual token. Evaluating at x=0 recovers v, and then W_q injectivity recovers k, so any prefix with v ≠ W_v W_k^{-1} k cannot be produced by a prompt. Numerically, the best soft-prompt fit to a random prefix has RMSE 1.03 against a target RMS of 2.38. At most the generic, all-architecture version is unproved here; calling it 'open' without citing these claims misleads experts.

(3) (f)'s example "e.g. W_q^T W_k ≠ 0" is neither sufficient nor necessary. With W_o=0 the head is constant for every prefix, even though W_q^T W_k ≠ 0 (numerical second difference 0.0). With W_q ≠ 0 and W_q^T W_k = 0, the prefix scores still vary with x, so the head is non-affine (second difference 3.43). The condition that matters is roughly W_q ≠ 0 and W_o ≠ 0, plus generic prefix keys and values.

(4) (d) writes the gate as g. The paper uses tanh(g_l), one gate per head, and the gate is zero-initialised. HF PEFT uses one raw scalar `adaption_gate` per layer, also zero-initialised, with no tanh. So the gate's range depends on the implementation. "One learned prompt" means one prompt P_l per adapted layer, and the text should say so.

(5) 'What this explains' says prefix methods "may struggle with tasks that need new attention patterns at the layer where the prefix acts". For deep prefixes (Li–Liang, P-tuning v2), the prefix acts at every layer, so read literally this contradicts the preceding clause. Accurate version: at the lowest prefixed layer the content attention equals the pretrained one exactly. Higher layers change only through their modified inputs, and per Petrov Sec. 6, to first order the change is only additive in each position, with no new bilinear query–key term.

safe_public_statement: For a fixed query, softmax attention is a monoid homomorphism into (normaliser, weighted value sum) followed by division. As a consequence, a prefix acts as an input-gated parallel adapter (He et al. 2022) that rescales, but never reorders, the content attention weights within its layer (Petrov–Torr–Bibi 2024). In contrast, LLaMA-Adapter's separate softmax with a zero-initialised gate leaves those weights exactly unchanged and is the identity at initialisation. In causal decoders with matching position offsets, every soft prompt is realised by a deep prefix (Li–Liang 2021; Petrov–Torr–Bibi 2024). For generic frozen weights a prefixed head is not affine even on single-token inputs, so prefix tuning cannot be folded into the head's own weights and has no neutral (identity) setting.
